item.title: Why Chebyshev’s Inequality Is Great: A Guarantee for Any Distribution
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Chebyshev’s inequality is great because it guarantees a minimum percentage of data within a certain number of standard deviations from the mean, regardless of the distribution’s shape. We do not need to assume the data follow a Normal bell curve, which makes it a universal safety net for unknown, skewed, or U-shaped datasets.

The Core Formula

For any distribution with a finite mean () and finite standard deviation (), the proportion of data within standard deviations of the mean () is at least

  • Within 2 standard deviations (): at least of the data.
  • Within 3 standard deviations (): at least of the data.

Example 1: Heavy-Tailed Data (Household Income)

Income data are skewed to the right because a few very high earners pull the tail far out, so a Normal distribution fits poorly.

Suppose a city reports a mean household income of with a standard deviation of . What is the minimum percentage of households earning between $30,000 and $90,000?

  1. Find . Both boundaries are $30,000 from the mean. Dividing by the standard deviation gives .
  2. Apply Chebyshev. .

Without seeing a single tax return, or knowing the shape of the income gap, we can guarantee that at least 75% of households earn between $30,000 and $90,000.

Example 2: Server Latency and SLA Guarantees

Software response times often follow irregular patterns with random spikes, yet companies must still sign strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

Suppose an API has a mean response time of ms and a standard deviation of ms. A client asks for the worst-case share of requests that take 160 ms or longer (or 40 ms or less).

  1. Find . 160 ms is 60 ms from the mean, and gives .
  2. Apply Chebyshev. At least of requests fall between 40 ms and 160 ms. Conversely, at most 11.1% fall outside this range.

Even if network traffic is erratic, the engineers can promise that no more than 11.1% of requests will breach the 160 ms limit (the bound counts both tails, so it is conservative for the slow side alone).

Chebyshev vs. the Normal Distribution

Distance from mean () Normal distribution (bell curve only) Chebyshev (any distribution)
1.5 86.6% at least 55.6%
2 95.4% at least 75.0%
3 99.7% at least 88.9%
4 99.99% at least 93.8%
Note

Chebyshev gives a very conservative lower bound. If we know the data are Normal, the Normal distribution gives much tighter estimates.

Testing It in R

Let’s test the inequality on three very different shapes: a Normal bell curve, a heavily right-skewed Exponential, and a polarised U-shaped Beta (see the U-shaped distribution post). For each, we compute the exact share of data within standard deviations of the mean. All three should stay above Chebyshev’s 75% minimum.

set.seed(123)
n <- 100000

# Three completely different distribution shapes
data_normal <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10)          # bell-shaped
data_skewed <- rexp(n, rate = 0.1)                   # heavily right-skewed
data_ushape <- rbeta(n, shape1 = 0.5, shape2 = 0.5)  # U-shaped

# Actual % of data within k standard deviations of the mean
check_chebyshev <- function(data, k = 2) {
  mu <- mean(data)
  sigma <- sd(data)
  actual_prop <- mean(data >= mu - k * sigma & data <= mu + k * sigma)
  round(actual_prop * 100, 2)
}

cat("Chebyshev minimum guarantee (k = 2): 75.00%\n")
Chebyshev minimum guarantee (k = 2): 75.00%
cat("Normal distribution actual:        ", check_chebyshev(data_normal), "%\n")
Normal distribution actual:         95.46 %
cat("Right-skewed (Exponential) actual: ", check_chebyshev(data_skewed), "%\n")
Right-skewed (Exponential) actual:  95.08 %
cat("U-shaped (Beta) actual:            ", check_chebyshev(data_ushape), "%\n")
U-shaped (Beta) actual:             100 %

All three comfortably exceed 75%. The bound is a floor valid for every distribution, not a typical value, so real data usually sit well above it.

Visualizing the Bounds

Here are the boundaries drawn over the skewed data.

library(ggplot2)

mu_skew <- mean(data_skewed)
sd_skew <- sd(data_skewed)

ggplot(data.frame(x = data_skewed), aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_skew, colour = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_skew + c(-2, 2) * sd_skew,
             colour = "red", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(title = "Chebyshev Bounds (k = 2) on Skewed Data",
       subtitle = "Blue: mean. Red dashed: mean ± 2 SD (about 95% of the data lie inside here)",
       x = "Value", y = "Count")

The lower boundary falls below zero, so only the upper line is visible, yet the guarantee still holds.

item.title: Area Charts in Statistics: Probability, Proportions and Cumulative Totals
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
An area chart fills the space under a line with colour. That emphasises the volume or magnitude of the data, not only the change from one point to the next. Statisticians use area charts for three main jobs: showing probability, showing proportions of a total, and showing cumulative totals. Let’s see each, with R.

1. Probability and Continuous Distributions

For a continuous random variable, the area under the density curve is probability, and the total area is (or ). Shading a region turns an abstract idea into something we can see.

  • P-values and significance. Shading the tails of a distribution shows the rejection region for a significance level .
  • Confidence and coverage. Shading the middle of a curve shows how much probability lies in an interval, such as the , and zones of the Empirical Rule.

Here is the two-sided rejection region of a standard normal test at . The critical values are .

library(tidyverse)

z <- tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 800), density = dnorm(x))
crit <- qnorm(0.975)   # 1.96

ggplot(z, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_area(data = filter(z, x <= -crit), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_area(data = filter(z, x >= crit),  fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Rejection region at alpha = 0.05 (shaded red)",
       x = "z", y = "Density")
# area in the two tails
2 * pnorm(-crit)
[1] 0.05

The two red tails together have area , which is the probability of a “significant” result when the null hypothesis is true.

2. Parts of a Total over Time: Stacked Area Charts

When a whole is made of several groups, a stacked area chart shows each group’s trend and the total at once. The top edge is the total, and the thickness of each band is that group’s contribution.

For example, here are made-up yearly emissions of a factory, split by pollutant.

set.seed(7)
emissions <- expand_grid(year = 2015:2025, pollutant = c("CO2", "NOx", "SO2")) %>%
  mutate(level = case_when(pollutant == "CO2" ~ 60, pollutant == "NOx" ~ 25, TRUE ~ 15) *
                 (1 - 0.02 * (year - 2015)) * runif(n(), 0.95, 1.05))

ggplot(emissions, aes(year, level, fill = pollutant)) +
  geom_area() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2025, 2)) +
  labs(title = "Factory emissions by pollutant (made-up data)",
       x = NULL, y = "Emissions (tonnes)", fill = NULL)

The total falls over the decade, and we can also see that CO2 is by far the largest part. A stacked area chart is best when the group order is fixed and the number of groups is small.

3. Cumulative Totals over Time

A line chart can hide the physical weight of accumulation. If the quantity adds up, such as rainfall during a season or the total number of cases in an outbreak, an area under the cumulative curve shows how much has built up.

set.seed(3)
rain <- tibble(day = 1:90, mm = rgamma(90, shape = 0.4, scale = 8)) %>%
  mutate(total = cumsum(mm))

ggplot(rain, aes(day, total)) +
  geom_area(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
  labs(title = "Accumulated rainfall over a 90-day season (simulated)",
       x = "Day", y = "Total rainfall (mm)")

Overlapping Areas: Use Transparency

Areas that are not stacked need care. If we draw two independent groups on the same axes with solid fills, the one drawn later hides part of the other (occlusion), and the chart misleads.

Transparency solves this for a few series. With a semi-transparent fill (alpha around 0.4), both areas stay visible, and the overlap shows as a darker blend. The panels below show the same data three ways: solid fills, transparent fills, and lines.

set.seed(11)
two <- tibble(x = rep(1:30, 2), group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 30)) %>%
  mutate(y = 50 + cumsum(rnorm(60, 0, 2)) + ifelse(group == "B", 8, 0))

solid <- ggplot(two, aes(x, y, fill = group)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Solid: B hides part of A", x = NULL, y = NULL)

transparent <- ggplot(two, aes(x, y, fill = group)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Transparent: both visible", x = NULL, y = NULL)

lines <- ggplot(two, aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Lines: clearest", x = NULL, y = NULL)

library(patchwork)
solid | transparent | lines

In the solid chart, group B is drawn on top and hides the lower part of group A, so we cannot tell where A’s area really starts or how the two compare. In the transparent chart, we can read both series, and the overlap is visible. A good habit is to add a line along the top edge of each area, so that each boundary stays crisp.

ggplot(two, aes(x, y, fill = group, colour = group)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "Transparent areas with outlines", x = NULL, y = NULL)

Transparency has limits. With three or more overlapping series, the blended colours become muddy and the overlaps are hard to decode. Then a line chart is the better choice.

Tip

Use an area chart when the filled amount itself means something: probability, a total or a cumulative quantity. For two overlapping series, make the fills transparent. If only the trend matters, or there are three or more unstacked series, use a line chart.

Summary

Use Chart What the area shows
Probability, p-values, intervals Area under a density curve Probability
Parts of a whole over time Stacked area Each group’s share and the total
Accumulation Cumulative area The total built up so far
Two overlapping series Transparent areas (with outlines) Each series, and where they overlap
Three or more separate series Not an area chart Use lines

item.title: When Are Bar Charts Useful? Six Cases with R Examples
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A bar chart maps each value to the length of a bar. Our eyes compare lengths very accurately, which is why bar charts are the safest choice whenever we compare quantities across distinct categories. Here are six situations where they work well, each drawn in R. The data are made up for illustration.

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

1. Comparing Categories (Nominal Data)

When categories have no natural order, we sort the bars by size so that the ranking is obvious. Typical uses are sales by product line or web traffic by referral source.

traffic <- tibble(
  source = c("Organic search", "Direct", "Social media", "Email", "Referral"),
  visits = c(5200, 3100, 2400, 1300, 900)
)

ggplot(traffic, aes(x = reorder(source, visits), y = visits)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Website visits by source", x = NULL, y = "Visits")

Pareto chart

A Pareto chart sorts the bars in descending order and adds a line with the cumulative percentage. It shows the “vital few” categories that cause most of an outcome, such as the common reasons for customer complaints.

complaints <- tibble(
  reason = c("Late delivery", "Damaged item", "Wrong item", "Billing error", "Rude staff", "Other"),
  n = c(120, 75, 40, 25, 15, 10)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  mutate(reason = fct_inorder(reason), cum_pct = cumsum(n) / sum(n) * 100)

total <- sum(complaints$n)

ggplot(complaints, aes(reason)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = n), fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = cum_pct * total / 100, group = 1), colour = "tomato", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cum_pct * total / 100), colour = "tomato", size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Complaints",
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / total * 100, name = "Cumulative %")) +
  labs(title = "Reasons for complaints (Pareto chart)", x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))

The first two reasons already account for over half of all complaints (68%), so that is where to act first.

2. Ordered Categories (Ordinal Data)

When categories follow a natural order, the bars keep that order. Likert survey answers are the classic case. We must keep the order of the scale, not sort by size.

likert <- tibble(
  answer = factor(c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree"),
                  levels = c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree")),
  n = c(12, 25, 38, 80, 45)
)

ggplot(likert, aes(answer, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Responses to a survey statement", x = NULL, y = "Respondents")

Income brackets (low, medium, high) or performance tiers work the same way.

3. Discrete Time Blocks

Line graphs suit measurements that flow continuously. When each value is a total for a block of time, such as monthly rainfall, quarterly earnings or daily steps, a bar chart is more honest: each bar is one block, and nothing is implied between them.

rain <- tibble(month = factor(month.abb, levels = month.abb),
               mm = c(8, 12, 30, 80, 190, 330, 360, 330, 250, 130, 20, 5))

ggplot(rain, aes(month, mm)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Monthly rainfall (made-up data)", x = NULL, y = "Rainfall (mm)")

Bars also suit a few time points, such as an indicator over 5 years, where a line over so few points looks sparse.

4. Parts of a Whole: Stacked Bars

To see the total and its parts, we can segment each bar. A stacked bar shows the totals. A 100% stacked bar shows the shares, whatever the totals.

energy <- expand_grid(country = c("A", "B", "C"), fuel = c("Coal", "Gas", "Solar")) %>%
  mutate(twh = c(60, 30, 10, 20, 50, 30, 10, 20, 70))

stacked <- ggplot(energy, aes(country, twh, fill = fuel)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Stacked: totals and parts", x = "Country", y = "Energy (TWh)", fill = NULL)

filled <- ggplot(energy, aes(country, twh, fill = fuel)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "100% stacked: shares", x = "Country", y = "Share", fill = NULL)

stacked | filled

A diverging stacked bar is a variant for survey scales. It centres the bars on the neutral answer, with negative answers to the left and positive ones to the right, so the net sentiment is visible at once.

5. Two Categorical Variables: Clustered Bars

To compare groups across a second variable, we put the bars side by side.

salary <- expand_grid(department = c("Sales", "IT", "HR"), status = c("Full-time", "Part-time")) %>%
  mutate(avg = c(52, 30, 61, 38, 48, 29))

ggplot(salary, aes(department, avg, fill = status)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Average salary by department and status",
       x = NULL, y = "Average salary (thousands)", fill = NULL)

6. Horizontal Bars

Rotating the chart by 90 degrees helps in two situations.

Long labels. Vertical bars force the labels to tilt, while horizontal bars keep them readable.

depts <- tibble(
  department = c("Department of Environmental Protection", "Department of Public Transport",
                 "Department of Health Services", "Department of Parks"),
  budget = c(42, 65, 90, 18)
)

ggplot(depts, aes(x = reorder(department, budget), y = budget)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Budget by department", x = NULL, y = "Budget (millions)")

Population pyramids. Two horizontal bar charts share a vertical age axis, with one group to the left and the other to the right.

pyramid <- expand_grid(age = c("0-14", "15-29", "30-44", "45-59", "60+"), sex = c("Male", "Female")) %>%
  mutate(pop = c(26, 24, 28, 27, 25, 25, 19, 20, 12, 15),
         pop = ifelse(sex == "Male", -pop, pop),
         age = factor(age, levels = c("0-14", "15-29", "30-44", "45-59", "60+")))

ggplot(pyramid, aes(age, pop, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = abs) +
  labs(title = "Population pyramid (made-up data)", x = "Age group", y = "Population (millions)", fill = NULL)

When to Choose a Bar Chart, and When Not To

Choose a bar chart if… Avoid a bar chart if…
The horizontal axis holds distinct groups, brackets or blocks of time The axis is a continuous scale (exact age, temperature, seconds): use a line plot or histogram
The goal is comparing exact differences in magnitude There are dozens of categories that clog the axis: use a sorted horizontal bar chart or a table
We want a chart that non-technical readers understand at once We want to show a distribution (spread, quartiles, outliers): use a box plot
Tip

Always start the value axis of a bar chart at zero. The bar’s length is the message, so a truncated axis exaggerates differences.

For a comparison with pie charts, see pie chart vs bar chart, and for choosing a chart by data type see choosing a chart by data type.

item.title: Choosing a Chart by Data Type: Categorical, Quantitative or Both
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
The right chart depends on the type of data in our variables. A wrong choice can distort a relationship, or show data in a way that makes no statistical sense, such as a line graph joining unrelated categories. Let’s go through the three cases and draw an example of each in R.

1. Categorical Data

Categorical (qualitative) data are labels or groups: gender, country, car model, satisfaction level. The usual goal is to compare counts or percentages across groups.

Chart Best for Example
Bar chart Comparing counts or percentages between separate groups Patients by blood type (, , , )
Stacked or grouped bar A main category split by a second one Agree / disagree answers by age group
Pie or donut chart Parts of a whole, with at most about five categories Market share of a few firms
Pareto chart Finding the few most frequent categories to prioritise Frequency of manufacturing defects

2. Quantitative Data

Quantitative (numerical) data are measurable quantities for which arithmetic makes sense. They are either discrete (countable, like shoe sizes or the number of children) or continuous (any value in a range, like height, time or weight).

Chart Best for Example
Histogram The distribution, spread and skewness of one continuous variable Household incomes in a city
Density or area chart A smooth distribution, or tail regions A normal curve and its critical region
Box plot Five-number summary and outliers Exam scores in one school
Line graph A change or trend over time Global temperature from 1880 to today
Scatter plot The relationship between two quantitative variables Hours studied and exam score

3. Mixed Data: Categorical and Quantitative

To see how a number behaves across groups, we use charts that combine both types:

  • Side-by-side box plots are the standard way to compare a quantitative variable across categories, for example salary across job titles.
  • Faceted histograms show a small histogram for each category, so that we can compare shape, centre and spread.

One Example of Each in R

We use the mpg data set that ships with ggplot2 (fuel economy of 234 cars). Each panel matches a row of the tables above. The plots use the default grey panel.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

bar <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = reorder(class, class, length))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Categorical: bar chart", x = NULL, y = "Number of cars")

hist <- ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Quantitative: histogram", x = "Highway mpg", y = "Number of cars")

scatter <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Two numbers: scatter", x = "Engine size (litres)", y = "Highway mpg")

line <- ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy / 1000)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Over time: line graph", x = NULL, y = "Unemployed (millions)")

box <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = reorder(drv, hwy, median), y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Mixed: box plot by group", x = "Drive type", y = "Highway mpg")

facet <- ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ drv, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Mixed: faceted histograms", x = "Highway mpg", y = "Cars")

(bar | hist | scatter) / (line | box | facet)

Notice what each chart answers. The bar chart ranks the categories, the histogram shows the shape of one variable, and the scatter plot shows how two variables move together. The line graph follows a change over time, while the box plot and the faceted histograms compare a number across groups.

Common Mistakes

  • A line graph for unordered categories. A line suggests a trend between points, so use bars for categories.
  • A pie chart with many slices. See pie chart vs bar chart and pie charts with many categories.
  • A histogram for categories, or a bar chart for a continuous variable. A histogram’s bars touch because the intervals are continuous, while the bars of a bar chart are separate.
Tip

Ask two questions first: what type is each variable, and what do we want to show (compare, see a distribution, follow a trend, or relate two variables)? The answers almost always point to one chart from the tables above.

Summary

We have We want Use
One categorical variable Compare counts Bar chart
One categorical variable Parts of a whole Pie or donut (few categories)
One quantitative variable See its distribution Histogram or box plot
Two quantitative variables See a relationship Scatter plot
A quantitative variable over time See a trend Line graph
Quantitative by categorical Compare groups Side-by-side box plots or faceted histograms

item.title: Can a Discrete Variable Have Fractional Values? Examples
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Many people think that a discrete variable must be a whole number, like the number of children. That is not the definition. A variable is discrete if it takes distinct, isolated values that can be counted, so that there is a gap between any two neighbouring allowed values. Those values may well be fractions or decimals.

What matters is not whether the numbers are whole, but whether values between two neighbours are possible.

Examples of Discrete Variables with Fractional Values

  • Shoe sizes. We can buy size 8, 8.5, 9 or 9.5, in steps of 0.5. A size 8.23 does not exist, so the set of values is separate and countable.
  • Stock prices before decimalisation. Before 2001, US stock exchanges quoted prices in fractions such as or of a dollar (for example or ). A price between two fractions was not allowed.
  • Pre-decimal British money. Before 1971, coins included the halfpenny (d) and the farthing (d). Prices moved in these fixed fractional steps.
  • Measuring cups. A standard set has , , and 1 cup. The capacity we can measure with one cup jumps from one of these fractions to the next.
  • Proportions with a fixed denominator. If we flip a coin 4 times, the proportion of heads can only be , , , or . A value like is impossible, because the denominator is fixed by .

Seeing the Last Example in R

For 4 coin flips, the number of heads follows a binomial distribution. Here are the probabilities of each possible proportion. The bars are separated, with nothing in between.

library(ggplot2)

flips <- data.frame(heads = 0:4)
flips$proportion <- flips$heads / 4
flips$probability <- dbinom(flips$heads, size = 4, prob = 0.5)
flips
  heads proportion probability
1     0       0.00      0.0625
2     1       0.25      0.2500
3     2       0.50      0.3750
4     3       0.75      0.2500
5     4       1.00      0.0625
ggplot(flips, aes(proportion, probability)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.05, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = flips$proportion, limits = c(-0.1, 1.1)) +
  labs(title = "Proportion of heads in 4 flips (discrete)",
       x = "Proportion of heads", y = "Probability")

Only five proportions can occur. If we had measured something continuous, such as the exact height of 4 people, any value in a range would be possible and the bars would merge into a curve.

Discrete or Continuous?

A useful test: can we always find another possible value between two given values? If yes, the variable is continuous. If no, it is discrete.

Variable type Value examples Countable and isolated?
Discrete (whole numbers) 1 child, 2 cars, 3 books Yes
Discrete (fractional) Size 7.5, size 8, size 8.5 Yes
Continuous 7.523 inches, 8.114 seconds No: infinitely many values between any two
Note

Measurements are often recorded in a discrete way. A person’s height is continuous, but when we write it to the nearest centimetre, the recorded values are discrete. It is the variable itself, not its rounding, that decides the type, so we classify height as continuous.

Summary

  • A discrete variable has separate, countable values with gaps between them.
  • Discrete does not mean whole numbers: shoe sizes, old stock prices and proportions of trials are all discrete fractions.
  • A variable is continuous when any value in a range is possible, with no gaps.

item.title: Is the Poisson Distribution Memoryless? Poisson vs Exponential
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A waiting time is memoryless if how long we have already waited tells us nothing about how much longer we will wait. Think of waiting for a random event, such as a call or a bus: after 20 minutes of waiting, we are no closer to the event than when we started. Does the Poisson distribution have this property?

Strictly speaking, the Poisson distribution itself is not memoryless. What is memoryless is the exponential distribution of the waiting time between events in a Poisson process. The two are closely linked, which is why they get confused. Let’s separate them.

What the Memoryless Property Means

A waiting time is memoryless if the past does not change the chance of a future outcome:

  • is the time we have already waited.
  • is the additional time we are asking about.

In plain words: if we have waited minutes and nothing has happened, the probability of waiting at least more minutes is exactly what it would be for someone who has just arrived. The process “forgets” how long it has run.

Poisson Count vs Exponential Waiting Time

Poisson Exponential
What it models The number of events in a fixed interval The waiting time between events
Type of variable Discrete (0, 1, 2, …) Continuous ()
Example Emails arriving in an hour Minutes between one email and the next
Memoryless? No Yes, and it is the only continuous distribution that is

The Poisson process has independent increments: counts in non-overlapping time windows do not affect each other. That is a different idea from memorylessness, which is a property of one waiting time.

If events arrive as a Poisson process with rate , the counts in a unit interval are Poisson(), and the waiting times between events are exponential with the same rate .

Checking the Memoryless Property in R

For an exponential waiting time, the probability of waiting longer than is . Let’s take a rate of events per minute (one event every 10 minutes on average), and ask: having waited minutes, what is the chance of waiting at least more?

rate <- 0.1
s <- 20
t <- 10

# P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > s + t) / P(X > s)
pexp(s + t, rate, lower.tail = FALSE) / pexp(s, rate, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 0.3678794
# P(X > t), for someone who has just arrived
pexp(t, rate, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 0.3678794

The two numbers are identical, . We can also check it by simulation, using only the waits that already exceeded :

set.seed(1)
waits <- rexp(1e6, rate)

mean(waits[waits > s] > s + t)   # among those who waited s, share who waited t more
[1] 0.3676605
mean(waits > t)                  # share of all waits longer than t
[1] 0.368468

Both are about , as the property says.

A Waiting Time That Is Not Memoryless

For contrast, think of a bus that comes on a timetable, every 30 minutes. If we arrive at a random moment, the wait is uniform from 0 to 30 minutes. Now the past matters.

library(tidyverse)

wait <- seq(0, 60, by = 0.5)
curves <- tibble(
  minutes = wait,
  Exponential = pexp(wait, 1 / 15, lower.tail = FALSE),
  Timetable   = punif(wait, 0, 30, lower.tail = FALSE)
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-minutes, names_to = "bus", values_to = "chance_still_waiting")

ggplot(curves, aes(minutes, chance_still_waiting, colour = bus)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Chance that we are still waiting after x minutes",
       x = "Minutes since we arrived", y = "Probability", colour = NULL)

For the timetable bus, once we have waited 20 minutes the bus is certain to come within 10 more. A new arrival could wait up to 30. The wait does depend on the past. For the exponential bus, the chance of waiting more minutes is the same no matter how long we have already waited.

Example: The Bus at a Random Stop

Suppose buses at a stop arrive at random, as a Poisson process, with per minute.

  • If we have already waited 20 minutes, the chance that we wait at least 10 more is .
  • A new passenger who has just walked up has exactly the same chance of waiting at least 10 minutes.
  • The bus does not become “due” because we have waited longer, and the process does not accumulate wear or memory.
Note

This is why waiting for a random event is frustrating. It is not that a long wait makes the event more likely. For truly random arrivals, the future is the same however long we have waited. A timetable is different, because there the past does carry information.

Summary

  • The Poisson distribution counts events in an interval, and is not memoryless.
  • The exponential distribution models the waiting time between those events, and is memoryless: .
  • It is the only continuous distribution with this property.
  • Related reading: Why Is the Poisson Distribution Used?

item.title: Normal Approximation to the Poisson Distribution (with R)
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A Poisson distribution can be approximated accurately by a normal distribution when the average rate is large. For small the Poisson is skewed to the right. As grows, the skew fades and the distribution becomes a symmetric bell. Let’s see when this works, how to use it, and how good it is. (For where the Poisson distribution comes from and what it is used for, see Why Is the Poisson Distribution Used?)

The Rule of Thumb

The approximation is reliable when:

  • for a rough, quick approximation, and
  • for good accuracy.

Matching the Parameters

A Poisson variable has mean and variance both equal to . We give the normal distribution the same mean and variance:

  • Mean:
  • Variance:
  • Standard deviation:

So, for large ,

The Continuity Correction

The Poisson counts whole numbers, but the normal distribution is continuous. To compensate, we move the boundary by , so that each whole number is represented by the interval from to .

Poisson probability Normal calculation

Example: Calls to a Call Centre

A call centre receives on average calls per hour. What is the probability of fewer than 20 calls in an hour?

Exact Poisson answer

“Fewer than 20” means :

Normal approximation

  1. Parameters: and .
  2. Continuity correction: becomes .
  3. Z-score:

  1. Table lookup: .

The approximation misses the exact value by only about .

Checking in R

# exact Poisson
ppois(19, lambda = 25)
[1] 0.1335748
# normal approximation, with continuity correction
pnorm(19.5, mean = 25, sd = 5)
[1] 0.1356661
# normal approximation, without the correction
pnorm(19, mean = 25, sd = 5)
[1] 0.1150697

Without the correction the answer is about , which is much farther from the exact . The correction is worth the extra half unit.

Watching the Poisson Become Normal

Let’s plot the Poisson probabilities (bars) for three values of , with the normal curve drawn over each.

library(tidyverse)

lambdas <- c(2, 7, 25)

# show each panel only over the range where the probability is not negligible
xrange <- function(l) c(max(0, l - 4 * sqrt(l) - 2), l + 4 * sqrt(l) + 2)

plot_data <- map_dfr(lambdas, function(l) {
  r <- xrange(l)
  tibble(lambda = l, x = ceiling(r[1]):floor(r[2]), poisson = dpois(x, l))
}) %>%
  mutate(label = factor(paste("lambda =", lambda), levels = paste("lambda =", lambdas)))

curve_data <- map_dfr(lambdas, function(l) {
  tibble(lambda = l, x = seq(xrange(l)[1], xrange(l)[2], length.out = 400),
         normal = dnorm(x, l, sqrt(l)))
}) %>%
  mutate(label = factor(paste("lambda =", lambda), levels = paste("lambda =", lambdas)))

ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = plot_data, aes(x, poisson), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x, normal), colour = "tomato", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Poisson (bars) and the normal curve N(λ, λ) (line)",
       x = "Number of events", y = "Probability")

What to look for:

  • : the peak is pressed against zero and the right tail is long. The normal curve even gives some probability to negative values, so it is a poor fit.
  • : the peak has moved away from zero and rounded off, but a slight skew to the right remains.
  • : the bars are centred and smooth, and the curve follows them closely.

How Good Is the Approximation?

One way to measure the error is the largest gap between the exact and approximate cumulative probabilities. We compare the normal approximation with and without the continuity correction.

max_error <- function(l, correction) {
  x <- 0:(3 * l + 10)
  shift <- if (correction) 0.5 else 0
  max(abs(ppois(x, l) - pnorm(x + shift, l, sqrt(l))))
}

tibble(lambda = c(2, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50)) %>%
  mutate(with_correction    = map_dbl(lambda, max_error, correction = TRUE),
         without_correction = map_dbl(lambda, max_error, correction = FALSE)) %>%
  mutate(across(-lambda, ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  knitr::kable()
lambda with_correction without_correction
2 0.0442 0.1767
5 0.0290 0.1160
10 0.0207 0.0830
20 0.0148 0.0591
25 0.0132 0.0529
50 0.0094 0.0375

Two things stand out. The error shrinks as grows, and it is always much smaller with the continuity correction. At the largest error with the correction is about , which supports the rule of thumb of .

Tip

For a single probability, check the exact value with ppois() or dpois() when software is available. The normal approximation is mainly useful for hand calculation, and for seeing why the bell shape appears.

Summary

  • Use when is large, say (a rough check is ).
  • Always apply the continuity correction of .
  • The approximation improves steadily as grows.

Related: Why Is the Poisson Distribution Used? covers real-world uses of the Poisson distribution and the conditions under which it fits.

item.title: Visualizing the Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7) in R

The Empirical Rule, also called the 68-95-99.7 rule, tells us how data spread around the mean when the distribution is bell-shaped (normal). Let’s state it, check it with a simulation in R, and then draw it.

An Example First

Suppose the marks of a large group of students are bell-shaped, with a mean of and a standard deviation of . The Empirical Rule then says:

  • about of the students score within one standard deviation of the mean: between and ,
  • about score within two standard deviations: between and ,
  • about , almost everyone, score within three standard deviations: between and .

So a mark below or above is very unusual: fewer than students in .

The Empirical Rule

For a normally distributed data set with mean and standard deviation :

Range Share of the data
about
about
about

So nearly all the data lie within three standard deviations of the mean, and values further away are rare.

Checking the Rule with Simulated Data

Let’s simulate exam marks like these, with mean and standard deviation , and measure the share of marks within one, two and three standard deviations.

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)
scores <- rnorm(n = 10000, mean = 70, sd = 5)

mean_val <- mean(scores)
sd_val   <- sd(scores)

within <- function(k) mean(scores >= mean_val - k * sd_val &
                           scores <= mean_val + k * sd_val) * 100

tibble(sd_range = c("1 SD", "2 SD", "3 SD"),
       simulated = round(map_dbl(1:3, within), 2),
       theory    = round((pnorm(1:3) - pnorm(-(1:3))) * 100, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable()
sd_range simulated theory
1 SD 68.29 68.27
2 SD 95.53 95.45
3 SD 99.73 99.73

The simulated percentages are very close to the theoretical ones. The theory column is exact: , and . The familiar , and are rounded versions of these.

Visualizing the Results

First, the histogram of the scores, with lines at one, two and three standard deviations from the mean.

breaks <- mean_val + (-3:3) * sd_val

ggplot(tibble(scores), aes(scores)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 1,
                 fill = "lightblue", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val),
                colour = "royalblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = breaks, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = round(breaks)) +
  labs(title = "10,000 simulated exam marks", x = "Mark", y = "Density")

Now the curve itself, with the three bands shaded. The darker the shade, the closer to the mean.

curve <- tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 800), density = dnorm(x))

ggplot(curve, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#cfe3f5") +
  geom_area(data = filter(curve, abs(x) <= 2), fill = "#8fbfe8") +
  geom_area(data = filter(curve, abs(x) <= 1), fill = "#4a90d9") +
  geom_line() +
  annotate("text", x = 0,    y = 0.15, label = "68%",   colour = "white", size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5,  y = 0.05, label = "95%",   size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.5, y = 0.05, label = "95%",   size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0,    y = 0.43, label = "99.7% lie within 3 SD", size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3, labels = c("-3σ", "-2σ", "-1σ", "μ", "+1σ", "+2σ", "+3σ")) +
  labs(title = "The Empirical Rule", x = NULL, y = "Density")

The “95%” labels mark the whole region within two standard deviations, which includes the central .

Warning

The rule applies to bell-shaped data. For skewed or heavy-tailed data the percentages can be quite different, so check the shape with a histogram first.

Summary

  • The Empirical Rule gives , and for one, two and three standard deviations.
  • A simulation with rnorm() confirms it: , and in our sample.
  • Shaded areas under the normal curve are the clearest way to show it.

item.title: Why Is the Poisson Distribution Used? Real-World Uses and Key Features
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Many real situations ask the same question: how many times will something happen in a fixed stretch of time or space? How many requests hit a server this second? How many accidents happen at a junction this month? How many customers walk in this hour? The Poisson distribution is the standard model for such counts. Let’s see where it is used, and then why it fits.

Where the Poisson Distribution Is Used

The recipe is always the same: events happen at random, at a steady average rate , and we count them in a fixed interval. The probability of seeing exactly events is

Field What we count Interval
Web and IT requests to a server, failed logins per second, per minute
Customer service calls to a call centre, customers at a till per hour
Health patients arriving at an emergency department per hour, per night
Insurance and safety accidents, claims, machine breakdowns per month, per year
Quality control defects in a roll of fabric, typos in a book per metre, per page
Science radioactive decays, stars in a patch of sky per second, per area
Ecology plants or animals in a quadrat per square metre
Sport goals in a football match per match

Let’s look at three of these in detail, with R.

1. Website traffic: planning server capacity

Scenario. A server receives on average requests per second. Engineers must decide how many requests it should handle per second. How often would a capacity of 20 requests per second be exceeded?

library(tidyverse)

lambda <- 12
traffic <- tibble(requests = 0:30, prob = dpois(requests, lambda)) %>%
  mutate(overload = requests > 20)

# probability of more than 20 requests in one second
ppois(20, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 0.01159774
ggplot(traffic, aes(requests, prob, fill = overload)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "steelblue", "TRUE" = "tomato"),
                    labels = c("Within capacity", "Overload (above 20)")) +
  labs(title = "Requests per second, Poisson(12)",
       x = "Requests in one second", y = "Probability", fill = NULL)

An overload is rare in any one second, but a server handles thousands of seconds a day, so even a small probability matters. The Poisson model lets us compute it from the average rate alone.

2. Accidents: pricing risk

Scenario. A junction averages accidents per month. An insurer wants the probability of a month with no accidents, and of a very bad month with 8 or more.

lambda <- 3.5

# exact probabilities
c(no_accident = dpois(0, lambda),
  eight_or_more = ppois(7, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE))
  no_accident eight_or_more 
   0.03019738    0.02673892

We can also simulate ten thousand months and check that the simulation agrees with the formula.

set.seed(42)
months <- tibble(accidents = rpois(10000, lambda))

mean(months$accidents == 0)   # simulated share of clean months
[1] 0.0323
months %>%
  count(accidents) %>%
  mutate(simulated = n / sum(n), exact = dpois(accidents, lambda)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(accidents)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = simulated), fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(y = exact), size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:12) +
  labs(title = "10,000 simulated months (bars) and the exact Poisson(3.5) (points)",
       x = "Accidents in a month", y = "Proportion of months")

3. Wildlife: are the plants scattered at random?

The Poisson distribution works in space as well as in time. Suppose we count orchids in 15 quadrats of one square metre each.

field <- c(2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 1, 4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1)   # orchids per quadrat

mean(field)
[1] 1.533333
var(field)
[1] 1.409524
# observed counts against the counts expected from a Poisson with the same mean
tibble(orchids = 0:4) %>%
  mutate(observed = map_int(orchids, ~ sum(field == .x)),
         expected = round(length(field) * dpois(orchids, mean(field)), 1))
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  orchids observed expected
    <int>    <int>    <dbl>
1       0        3      3.2
2       1        5      5  
3       2        4      3.8
4       3        2      1.9
5       4        1      0.7

If the plants are scattered completely at random, the counts per quadrat follow a Poisson distribution, so the variance is close to the mean. If they cluster, the variance is much larger than the mean. Here the two are close, and the observed counts are near the expected ones, so these orchids look randomly scattered. (With only 15 quadrats this is a rough check, not a proof.)

Why It Fits: The Conditions and Features

The Poisson distribution is a good model when:

  1. Events are independent. One event happening does not change the chance of the next. A call arriving does not make another call more or less likely.
  2. The average rate is steady. The rate is the same across the interval. A call centre with a lunchtime rush does not have a constant rate over the whole day, so we model shorter periods separately.
  3. Events occur one at a time. Two events almost never happen at exactly the same instant.
  4. We only count events. There is no fixed number of trials. Unlike the binomial distribution, we do not need to know a maximum , and the count can in principle be any whole number.

What follows from these conditions:

  • One parameter. The average rate is all we need to know.
  • The mean equals the variance. Both are . This gives a quick check on real data: if the variance is much larger than the mean, the Poisson model is a poor fit (the counts are “overdispersed”, often because events cluster).
  • Skewed for small , bell-shaped for large . See the normal approximation.
  • Close to the binomial for rare events. See when a binomial can be approximated by a Poisson.
Note

The “memoryless” property that is sometimes mentioned belongs to the waiting time between events, which follows the exponential distribution, and not to the Poisson count itself. If events occur as a Poisson process, the wait until the next event does not depend on how long we have already waited.

Checking the Mean and Variance in R

Here is the check in practice. For real Poisson data the variance is close to the mean, and for clustered data it is not.

set.seed(1)
poisson_data   <- rpois(1000, 4)
clustered_data <- rnbinom(1000, mu = 4, size = 1)   # events that cluster

c(mean = mean(poisson_data),   variance = var(poisson_data))
    mean variance 
4.018000 4.057734 
c(mean = mean(clustered_data), variance = var(clustered_data))
    mean variance 
 4.11400 19.92092

The first pair is close, which supports a Poisson model. The second has a variance several times the mean, so a Poisson model would underestimate how variable the counts are.

Summary

  • The Poisson distribution models counts of random events in a fixed time or space, at a steady average rate.
  • It appears in IT traffic, call centres, hospitals, insurance, quality control, science and ecology.
  • It needs only one parameter, , which is both the mean and the variance.
  • It fits when events are independent and the rate is steady. If the variance is far above the mean, look for another model.

Related: for large the Poisson looks like a normal curve, see Normal Approximation to the Poisson Distribution.

A binomial distribution can be approximated reliably by a Poisson distribution when the number of trials is large and the probability of success is small. In other words, the approximation suits rare events counted over many trials. Let’s see the rule, two worked examples, and a picture of how good the fit is.

Why It Works

The binomial probability of successes is

The Rule of Thumb

When these hold, we take the Poisson mean as .

The two variances are nearly equal exactly when , that is, when is small. This is another way to see why a small is needed.

Example 1: Product Defects

A factory produces lightbulbs with a defect rate of 2% (). We inspect a random sample of bulbs. What is the probability that exactly 3 are defective?

The probability that a page has a major printing error is 0.5% (). In a book of pages, what is the probability that at most 1 page has an error?

Setup: .

Poisson:

The difference is only about .

Checking Both Examples in R

dbinom() and dpois() give the exact probabilities, and pbinom() and ppois() the cumulative ones.

# Example 1: P(X = 3), n = 100, p = 0.02
c(binomial = dbinom(3, 100, 0.02), poisson = dpois(3, 2))
 binomial   poisson 
0.1822759 0.1804470 
# Example 2: P(X <= 1), n = 500, p = 0.005
c(binomial = pbinom(1, 500, 0.005), poisson = ppois(1, 2.5))
